main.t: A small U-shaped bone in the upper neck that touches no other bone (hyoid bone).

simpler.t: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone in your neck, below your jaw.

deeper.t: It is the base of the tongue, and it moves when you swallow and speak.

facts.t: It lies in the upper neck, near the level of the lower edge of the mandible.
The tips of the U point backwards.
It is not part of the skull: it does not touch any other bone.

simpler.t: It sits at the top of your neck, just under your jaw.

deeper.t: A ligament from the styloid process of the temporal bone helps support it.

items.name: U shape
items.t: A small curved bone, open at the back.

items.name: Tips
items.t: The two ends of the U, pointing backwards.

items.name: Muscle attachments
items.t: Small muscles attach to it from above and from below.

items.name: Ligament attachment
items.t: A ligament from the styloid process of the temporal bone supports it.

simpler.t: It is a small U of bone, held in place by muscles.

deeper.t: It is one of the very few bones that join no other bone.

facts.t: Held only by muscles and a ligament, it can move up, down, forwards and back.
It forms a base for the tongue above and is attached to the larynx below.
Its movements are coordinated with the tongue, larynx and pharynx in swallowing and speaking.

simpler.t: It hangs in the neck on muscles and helps you swallow and talk.

items.name: Styloid process of the temporal bone
items.t: Gives off a ligament that supports the hyoid.

items.name: Small muscles of the neck
items.t: Attach from above and below, moving it up, down, forwards and back.

simpler.t: The tongue sits on it, and the larynx and pharynx are attached to it.

facts.t: It forms from cartilage of the second and third pharyngeal arches.

items.injury: Strong pressure on the front of the neck, as in strangulation.
items.why: The hyoid moves with the tongue, larynx and pharynx in swallowing and speaking.
items.check: A fracture of the hyoid is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); its role in swallowing and speech is.

items.injury: Weakness of the small muscles attached to the hyoid, for example after a stroke.
items.damaged: The muscles that move the hyoid.
items.cannotDo: Swallow safely: food may enter the airway.
items.why: Swallowing needs the hyoid to move in step with the larynx and pharynx.
items.check: Swallowing problems after a stroke are not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the hyoid’s role is.

items.q: Explain how the hyoid can move, although it touches no other bone.
model: It is held in position by small muscles that attach from above and below.
A ligament from the styloid process also supports it.
With no joint to another bone, it is free to move.
The muscles move it up, down, forwards and back.

items.q: Compare the hyoid bone with the bones of the skull.
model: The 22 skull bones are joined; 21 are united by sutures, and the mandible moves at its joint.
The hyoid touches no other bone.
So it is not part of the skull.
It is held in place by muscles and a ligament instead.

items.q: Place your fingers under your jaw and swallow. Predict what you feel, and explain why.
model: Muscles attached to it pull it during swallowing.
It moves in step with the tongue, larynx and pharynx.
The larynx, attached below it, moves too.

check.stem: Which bone does the hyoid touch?
check.why: It is an independent bone that does not contact any other bone.

check.stem: What shape is the hyoid bone?
check.why: It is a small U-shaped bone.

check.stem: What does the hyoid form a base for?
check.why: It serves as the base for the tongue above; the larynx and pharynx are attached to it.
